title: The Badger Who Wouldn't Budge
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks of Aeridor touched the clouds, and from them Wizard Quill’s tower, a needle of stone and starlight, reached for the heavens. Below, valleys spread like emerald carpets. Ancient wind whispered secrets over sharp ridgelines. Perched on Quill’s shoulder, a jackdaw named Quip tilted his head, bright eyes sharp with curiosity. Quip’s vocabulary was mostly thoughtful squawks and a knack for finding lost buttons.

“Patience now, Quip,” Quill murmured, arranging shimmering vials in his sunlit workshop. “Order is the first spell. Without it, even potent magic unravels.”

Quip offered a short affirming squawk and ruffled glossy black feathers.

A whirlwind of frantic energy burst through the tower door. Elara, a villager whose apron was alarmingly askew, scrambled up the winding stone steps.

“Wizard! Oh, Wizard Quill! It’s Bartholomew! He’s just stopped! Right in the middle of the Sunstone Pass. And he will not budge!”

Bartholomew. Elara’s beloved badger, usually content with root-digging and sun-drenched naps.

Quill’s eyebrows, usually lost in his grey hair, rose. “Stopped? Not by any spell?”

“No!” Elara wrung her hands. “He’s just decided. The kingdom’s grain cart is trapped! Bartholomew is blocking the way!”

Quill, a man of calm order, felt an unusual prickle of excitement. A puzzle of simple unvarnished will. His magic lay in understanding, not thunderbolts. He smoothed his robes.

“Right then. Let us go and observe this monumental Bartholomew.”

He looked at Quip, whose beady eyes blinked with ancient knowing. Quip was more than a bird. An extension of Quill’s own mind.

“You, my fine feathered fellow, are precisely the familiar a wizard needs.”

Quip puffed his chest. A proud squawk that meant, naturally.

Elara led. Quill followed, purposeful on the winding mountain path. Ancient pines cast shadows like dark ribbons. As they climbed, a figure emerged from a moss-covered cottage. Steam curled from a cauldron over a crackling fire. Witch Juniper, stirring with a gnarled stick, voice like stones tumbling in a clear stream.

“Ah, Quill. Off to wrestle with a recalcitrant rodent?”

“A badger, Juniper. Bartholomew. Blocking the Sunstone Pass.”

A low dry chuckle. Eyes twinkling. “That badger has a mind as solid as granite. And I suspect his stubbornness has more to do with what’s under the stone than what’s on top.”

Quill pondered, respecting her sharp wit. They reached the Sunstone Pass.

There he was. Bartholomew. A stout brown badger, planted firmly in the centre of the path, claws dug deep. He wasn’t growling. He simply was. A monumental obstacle. The grain cart sat behind him, its driver wringing his hands.

“Bartholomew!” Elara’s voice cracked. “Please, dear boy. Just a little step.”

An ear twitched. He remained immobile.

Quill stepped forward, calm determination radiating. He pulled out a shimmering orb. “A little something to brighten your day.” He tapped it, conjuring visions of sunshine and plump grubs. Bartholomew yawned, a wide cavern of indifference.

Next, a playful butterfly, wings woven from moonlight, danced before the badger’s nose. Bartholomew squinted, then went back to being an immovable object.

Impatience nudged. Then Juniper’s words returned: under the stone. Quill knelt, ignoring dust on his robes, and examined the ground with a magnifying lens. Quip landed on a nearby boulder, watching with keen interest.

Pine shadows stretched long and cool. Quill’s sharp eyes found it. A small dark patch of earth beside Bartholomew. Recently disturbed. Peeking out: the unmistakable tip of a forlorn-looking turnip. Bartholomew wasn’t blocking the pass out of malice. He was guarding a secret snack.

“Ah.” A slow smile. The ordinary idea. He did not need a thunderbolt. He needed a garden trowel.

He beckoned to Elara. “Do you happen to have any more of these excellent turnips?”

Bewildered but hopeful, she rummaged in her basket and produced a small bumpy one. With gentle hands Quill dug a small inviting hole next to Bartholomew, placed the new turnip in it, and patted the earth softly.

Bartholomew watched, dark eyes following. Then, with a sigh, he lumbered a single significant step to the side. He nudged the new turnip with his damp nose and began to dig with contented purpose.

The grain cart rumbled past with a grateful clatter. Its driver let out a relieved whoop.

“That badger,” declared Witch Juniper, who had reappeared as if summoned by solved problems, “is attempting subtlety. It is not its strongest subject.”

Quill smiled, dusting off his hands. Quip landed softly on his shoulder and nudged his ear. A chirp that Quill understood perfectly: well done. Now, about that shiny button glinting near Juniper’s cauldron.

Quill chuckled. The sun dipped below the ridgelines, apricot and rose. The pass was a pass again. Bartholomew, who would not budge for visions or moonlight butterflies, budged for a turnip, which was, when you thought about it, a kind of magic that did not need a name.
characters: Quill (orderly wizard of Aeridor), Quip (button-finding jackdaw), Juniper (witch of the moss cottage)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
